'''''Soto mie''''',<ref name="IndonesiaKaya">{{cite web |url=http://www.indonesiakaya.com/kanal/detail/soto-mie-bogor |title=Soto Mie Bogor |publisher=Indonesia Kaya |language=id |access-date=11 August 2014}}</ref> '''''Soto mi''''', or '''''Mee soto'''''<ref>{{cite web |url= http://thestar.com.my/news/story.asp?file=%2F2006%2F6%2F26%2Fcentral%2F14585503&sec=central |title= Little touches for unique dishes |author= Geetha Krishnan |date= 26 June 2006 |publisher= [[The Star (Malaysia)]] |access-date= 19 April 2026 |url-status=dead
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110622000920/http://thestar.com.my/news/story.asp?file=%2F2006%2F6%2F26%2Fcentral%2F14585503&sec=central |archive-date= 22 June 2011 }}</ref>
is a spicy [[Indonesian cuisine|Indonesian]] [[noodle soup]] dish<ref>{{cite book | last1=Whitmarsh | first1=A. | last2=Wood | first2=M. | title=Jakarta: 25 Excursions in and Around the Indonesian Capital | publisher=Tuttle Publishing | year=2013 | isbn=978-1-4629-0893-6 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nhTRAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT119 | access-date=1 February 2015 | page=119}}</ref> commonly found in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. ''Mie'' means [[noodle]] made of flour, salt and egg, while ''[[soto (food)|soto]]'' refers to [[List of Indonesian soups|Indonesian]] soup. In Indonesia, it is called ''soto mie'' and is considered one variant of ''[[soto (food)|soto]]'', while in [[Malaysia]] and [[Singapore]] it is called ''mee soto''.
